name: Beagle 2
title: Beagle 2: the lander that went quiet
note: Illustrations are AI-generated artwork based on the verified events; every fact and its source come from the research dossiers. Narration is written for short, clear audio (~50 words).

closing.title: thank you, Beagle 2
closing.text: A British lander built on a tiny budget reached Mars in 2003 and was found in 2015, less than two meters wide.

parts.title: Earth
parts.blurb: Before Mars: a bold idea, a tiny budget, a launch and a release, told as a comic.

parts.title: Mars
parts.blurb: Twelve moments around a silent lander on Isidis Planitia: Beagle 2 never moves, so press Space to go from one moment to the next.

beats.title: A lander for Mars Express
beats.summary: British scientist Colin Pillinger convinces ESA to add a lander to its first Mars mission, and names it after Darwin's ship.
beats.narration: Nineteen ninety-seven. Planetary scientist Colin Pillinger, of the Open University in Britain, thinks Europe's first Mars mission is missing something: a lander. He convinces the European Space Agency to add one, and names it Beagle 2, after Darwin's ship. The whole project gets about forty-five million pounds, a fraction of NASA's missions.

beats.title: One of three proposals
beats.summary: ESA invites proposals for a lander and picks Beagle 2 out of three. The deadline is set by the planets: Mars will be closest in summer 2003.
beats.narration: The European Space Agency invites teams to propose a lander for Mars Express. Three proposals reach the table, and it picks Beagle 2. The planets set the deadline: in summer 2003 Mars will be at its closest to Earth, and that launch window cannot be missed. Weight, money and time are tight.

beats.title: Named after Darwin's ship
beats.summary: Not an acronym but the HMS Beagle. An artist paints the dot chart that calibrates its instruments, and a rock band writes its call signal.
beats.narration: Pillinger skips the usual acronym and names the lander after the HMS Beagle, the ship that carried Charles Darwin. Darwin sought the origins of life on Earth; Beagle 2 will look for life on Mars. Artist Damien Hirst paints a chart of colored dots to calibrate its instruments, and the band Blur writes its call signal.

beats.title: A lab in sixty kilograms
beats.summary: A one-meter robotic arm carries cameras, a microscope, two spectrometers and a drill; a mole can dig 1.5 meters down. A whole laboratory, miniaturized.
beats.narration: The contest sets a limit of sixty kilograms for the lander, and Pillinger says Beagle was the only viable option. Everything hangs on a one-meter robotic arm, the PAW, with cameras, a microscope, two spectrometers and a drill. A small digging mole, PLUTO, can go one and a half meters down. It is a whole laboratory, miniaturized.

beats.title: Liftoff from Baikonur
beats.summary: A Soyuz-Fregat rocket lifts off from Kazakhstan with Mars Express and Beagle 2: 400 million kilometers and six months to Mars.
beats.narration: June second, 2003, at a quarter to midnight. A Soyuz-Fregat rocket lifts off from Baikonur, in Kazakhstan, carrying Mars Express, Europe's first mission to another planet. Strapped to it rides Beagle 2. The launch window opens only every twenty-six months. The journey is four hundred million kilometers and six months long.

beats.title: Let go, spinning
beats.summary: Mars Express releases Beagle 2 with a spring, spinning like a top. The lander has no engine of its own, so its path was set beforehand.
beats.narration: December nineteenth, 2003. Mars Express releases Beagle 2. A spring pushes it away, spinning like a top to stay stable. The lander has no engine to correct its course, so its path was set with great precision beforehand. Two minutes later, the orbiter's camera takes the last picture of it, a small dot drifting away.

beats.title: Christmas silence
beats.summary: Mars Express enters orbit perfectly on the day Beagle 2 should land. The first radio contact never comes, and the screens stay silent.
beats.narration: December twenty-fifth, 2003, Christmas Day. Mars Express enters orbit around Mars, perfectly. It is also the day Beagle 2 should land. The first radio contact, expected soon after, never comes. In the control rooms, the screens stay silent. Over the next weeks, many attempts end the same way.

beats.title: What they hoped to hear
beats.summary: The first sign should have been nine notes by Blur. Then 13 more tries and a slow beacon: ten seconds on, fifty off, with five watts of power.
beats.narration: What the team expected on Christmas Day was nine notes by the band Blur. If that failed, the lander had thirteen more scheduled tries with NASA's Mars Odyssey, then a slow backup beacon: ten seconds on, fifty off. Its transmitter had five watts, about as much as a mobile phone.

beats.title: A crater in the landing zone
beats.summary: A NASA orbiter picture shows a 1-kilometer crater right in the middle of the landing ellipse, which had shrunk from 480 × 300 km to 70 × 10 km.
beats.narration: December twenty-ninth, 2003. A picture from NASA's Mars Global Surveyor, taken twenty minutes after the planned landing, shows a crater about one kilometer wide in the middle of the landing zone. Pillinger compares it to Arizona's Meteor Crater. The ellipse had shrunk from four hundred eighty by three hundred kilometers to seventy by ten.

beats.title: The last resort
beats.summary: Three days of searching with two orbiters and a radio telescope end in silence. One idea remains: a «hail» command sent by Mars Odyssey.
beats.narration: January twenty-sixth, 2004. Three days of intense searching with Mars Express, Mars Odyssey and the Jodrell Bank radio telescope end in silence. By now the lander should be in an emergency mode with its receiver always on. The likely explanation: a nearly flat battery. One last idea remains: a hail command, sent by Odyssey the next day.

beats.title: Declared lost
beats.summary: In London, the Beagle 2 management board formally declares the lander lost. An official inquiry is announced days later.
beats.narration: February sixth, 2004. In London, the Beagle 2 management board meets and formally declares the lander lost. More than a month has passed since the planned landing without a single signal. A few days later, British science minister Lord Sainsbury and the European Space Agency announce an official inquiry into the failure.

beats.title: Searching strip by strip
beats.summary: NASA's Mars Global Surveyor photographs over a third of the landing ellipse at 1.5 meters per pixel. The one dark candidate is not the lander.
beats.narration: January to April, 2004. NASA's Mars Global Surveyor searches the landing ellipse at one and a half meters per pixel. By April it has covered over a third of the area. Only one candidate stands out: a dark spot about twenty meters wide. A sharper look shows an old crater, not a lander.

beats.title: An instrument, not a spacecraft
beats.summary: The inquiry finds no single technical cause. It finds that Beagle 2 was managed like an instrument, with fewer controls than a spacecraft needs.
beats.narration: April, 2004. The inquiry delivers its report. It cannot name one technical cause. Instead it finds organizational reasons that raised the risk: Beagle 2 was treated like an instrument, not like a spacecraft that must survive alone on another planet. The window was fixed, time was short, and the report makes nineteen recommendations.

beats.title: Eight years, 26 photos
beats.summary: Only one camera is sharp enough to find a 1.5-meter lander: HiRISE. Twenty-six of its images of the area show nothing.
beats.narration: From 2006 to 2014, nothing turns up. The ellipse has been narrowed to a fifty-seven kilometer axis, still over fourteen hundred square kilometers, and the lander is just one and a half meters wide. The only camera sharp enough, HiRISE on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, takes twenty-six images of the area without finding a trace.

beats.title: A photo already in the archive
beats.summary: HiRISE photographs the middle of the landing zone. Nobody knows it, but the lander may already be in the frame.
beats.narration: February twenty-eighth, 2013. HiRISE takes a picture of the middle of Beagle 2's landing zone, at twenty-eight centimeters per pixel. Nobody knows it, but the lander may already be in the frame. The image sits in the archive of the University of Arizona. A second picture, in June 2014, will let scientists compare the two.

beats.title: The leader is gone
beats.summary: Colin Pillinger dies at 70, months before his lander is found. He never learns where it ended up.
beats.narration: May seventh, 2014. Colin Pillinger dies at seventy, two days before his birthday. His career began in 1968 analyzing Apollo moon samples. The European Space Agency called him the driving force behind Beagle 2, a lander that cost about forty million dollars, when NASA's Viking landers had cost a billion. He never learns where his lander is.

beats.title: A citizen scientist's lead
beats.summary: Michael Croon, a former Mars Express team member, asks for a picture through HiRISE's public program and spots a bright point at the frame's edge.
beats.narration: January, 2015. Michael Croon, a German amateur and former Mars Express operations team member, uses HiRISE's public request program, HiWish, to ask for a picture of the landing zone. Comparing images from 2013 and 2014, he spots a bright point at the edge of the frame. It leads to the first sight of Beagle 2.

beats.title: Found on the surface
beats.summary: HiRISE shows Beagle 2 on the plain, more than eleven years after it vanished, with its panels at least partly open.
beats.narration: January, 2015. HiRISE shows Beagle 2 on the surface, more than eleven years after it vanished, with its solar panels at least partly open. A second picture, in different sunlight, shows glints in other places: more than one open panel. Nearby lie its back cover with the small parachute, and the main parachute.

beats.title: It landed, but did not call
beats.summary: NASA and the UK Space Agency announce it: the landing worked. A panel that stayed closed may have blocked the antenna.
beats.narration: January sixteenth, 2015. NASA and the UK Space Agency announce it: Beagle 2 reached the surface on Christmas Day, 2003, as planned. The entry, descent and landing had worked. But the radio antenna only comes out when all four panels open. The images suggest at least one stayed closed, which would explain eleven years of silence.

beats.title: «It hit the crossbar»
beats.summary: Pillinger's widow speaks of immense pride and great sadness: the lander almost made it. In football terms, it hit the crossbar.
beats.narration: January, 2015. Colin Pillinger's widow, Doctor Judith Pillinger, speaks of immense pride tinged with great sadness, because Colin could not share the news. Beagle 2, she says, hit the crossbar: it almost made it. It was not a plain failure or a success, but a small British lander that touched Mars on a very tight budget.
